processing: The best-known style is flat and sword-shaped: the leaf is heated to stop oxidation, then pressed flat and dried. The name also covers other grades and shapes sold as Maojian and Xueya.
harvest_season: Specific dates are not well recorded. As is usual for Sichuan mountain greens, early spring pickings are the most sought after.
appearance_dry: Flat, sword-like leaves with a smooth, jade-green colour.
appearance_wet: Tender, whole leaves in bright yellow-green.
taste_profile: Fresh and rich with a sweet aftertaste, carrying a long gentle aroma that can lean floral.

brewing.notes: Use an open vessel or lift the lid after pouring, so the leaf does not stew in its own heat.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring tea and best drunk within about a year, as with other Chinese greens. The protected name covers all of Wangcang County, and several grades and shapes share it, so check the picking date and the grade name.
description:
Micangshan tea comes from Wangcang County in Guangyuan, grown in the Micang Mountains on the border zone between China's northern and southern climates. It is counted among Sichuan's ten famous teas, a provincial title awarded in 2006, and is one of the better-known names of the northern part of the province.

The classic form is flat and sword-shaped, with a jade tone. Gardens are in the mountains, with rainfall above 1200 mm a year and an average temperature near 15°C, a cool and damp setting of the sort green tea growers look for.

The cup is yellow-green and bright, with a fresh, full flavour and a sweet finish. Its aroma is long rather than loud. Water around 85°C and a first steep of about a minute will show that off without bitterness.

Buying is mainly about reading the label. The name is an appellation across the whole county, and products such as Maojian and Xueya come under it, while a large local company also trades on the mountain's name. Look for this year's spring date and a named grade.
history:
Local stories credit the tea's fame to early figures: a Han king who drank it before a victory, Zhuge Liang stationing troops on the mountain and lending it its name, and Empress Wu Zetian favouring it. These are legends, not records.

The documented history is modern. A provincial tea group was set up in the early 2000s to industrialise production, the tea was named one of Sichuan's ten famous teas in 2006, and national geographical indication protection was approved on 4 May 2009.
